newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil complex ends higher on Iraq conflict.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil complex ends higher on Iraq conflict.

text.p: All three legs of the NYMEX oil complex ended higher after reaching life-of-contract highs in the spot month in a rally sparked by news Iraq fired missiles at U.S. jets in northern Iraq, traders said.
"The market is worried that the tension in Iraq could escalate even more every time the U.S. flies over the no-fly zone," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products at Paribas Futures Inc.
U.S. jets were patrolling a "no-fly" zone set by the United States and allied forces after the 1991 Gulf War.
October crude settled up 63 cents at $24.75 a barrel.
October crude reached a life-of-contract high Wednesday of $24.98. The post-Gulf War high for crude is $25.70.

"This just delays the oil-for-food deal further but it's broader than that. There is a conflict in an oil rich region," said a trader of the tensions in Iraq. The Middle East is the key supplier of the world's oil.

October heating oil rose to a contract high of 68.60 cents a gallon, but pulled back to settle at 68.19 cents, up 1.52 cents a gallon. The latest inventory data by the American Petroleum Institute (API) indicates distillate stocks remain tight, with stocks 17.1 million barrels below a year ago.
October gasoline ended 1.06 cents higher at 65.91 cents a gallon, but rose during the session to a life-of-contract high of 66.70 cents a gallon.
Traders said gasoline followed crude and heating oil higher on the Iraq news. However, heating oil's fundamentals sharpened its rally.
"When I talk to clients all, I hear is stocks are 50 percent below a year ago in Padd 1," said a trader of heating oil's price rise.

For the week ended September 6, API said low-sulfur distillate stocks in Padd 1, or northeastern United States, were 20.9 million barrels compared to 40.3 million barrels a year ago. Padd 1 is the world's largest market for heating oil.

Oil prices have been strong since last week after the United Nations suspended the oil-for-food deal with Iraq in response to military incursions by Saddam Hussein's forces into Kurdish regions in northern Iraq.
"Prices could consolidate, but it depends on the developments in Iraq," said a trader.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
